description: Classifying data: quantitative, qualitative, discrete, continuous, bivariate and the explanatory/response variable pair.
content_html:
Why Classifying Data Matters

Before you can choose a graph, a formula, or a statistical test, you need to know what type of data you have. A bar chart is right for some data but completely wrong for others. The mean makes sense for some measurements but is meaningless for others. Every decision in the rest of your investigation flows from the type of data you collected. Getting this classification right at the start prevents wasted effort later.

Quantitative and Qualitative Data

Quantitative data is data that takes numerical values. Height in centimetres, temperature in degrees, number of goals scored — all of these are quantitative because you can do arithmetic with them. Calculating the mean height or the total goals scored is meaningful.

Qualitative data describes qualities or categories. Eye colour, favourite genre of music, a person’s opinion expressed in their own words — these are qualitative. You cannot calculate a meaningful mean eye colour. Qualitative data is often ‘words’ rather than numbers, though it can be coded into numbers (1 = strongly agree, 5 = strongly disagree) — but even then, the codes are labels, not measurements.

Key Fact

The key test: can you do meaningful arithmetic with the values? If yes, the data is quantitative. If no (e.g. averaging “nationalities” makes no sense), it is qualitative.

Categorical and Ordinal Data

Within qualitative data, two further types matter. Categorical data falls into groups with no natural ordering. Blood group (A, B, AB, O), country of birth, and make of car are categorical — there is no sensible way to say that blood group B comes ‘after’ blood group A.

Ordinal data can be ordered or ranked, but the gaps between positions are not equal. Placing first, second, or third in a race is ordinal — you know the order, but ‘first is better than second’ does not tell you by how much. Survey responses such as “poor / fair / good / excellent” are ordinal: the order is clear, but the step from ‘poor’ to ‘fair’ is not necessarily the same size as the step from ‘good’ to ‘excellent’.

Discrete and Continuous Data

Within quantitative data, two further types are essential. Discrete data can only take specific, separate values. The number of students in a class is discrete: you can have 28 or 29 students, but not 28.4. The number of goals in a match is discrete.

Continuous data can take any value within a range. Height, weight, temperature, and time are all continuous — a student’s height could theoretically be 163.47 cm. In practice, measurement tools limit the precision, but the underlying characteristic is continuous.

Why does this distinction matter? Discrete data is usually represented with bar charts and pictograms (with gaps between bars). Continuous data is represented with histograms (no gaps), or can be grouped into class intervals. You should choose the representation that matches the data type, not the one that looks nicest.

Students often argue about shoe size. In the UK, shoe sizes come in specific values (6, 6.5, 7, 7.5, ...) — there is no UK size 7.3. That makes shoe size discrete, even though it is a numerical measurement.

Contrast this with foot length in centimetres. That is continuous — a foot could be 26.2 cm or 26.25 cm. The key question is whether the measuring system has genuine gaps between values, or whether it is just rounding a continuous thing. Shoe sizes are a labelling convention, so they are discrete. Foot lengths are continuous.

Ungrouped and Grouped Data

Data can also be described as ungrouped (individual values listed separately) or grouped (values collected into class intervals). Grouping is useful when a dataset is large and spread over a wide range — it makes patterns easier to see. However, grouping loses precision: once data is grouped, you can only estimate the mean, not calculate it exactly.

When creating class intervals, check that they do not overlap and that they cover the full range of the data. The choice of class width affects how clearly the distribution is visible: too many narrow classes and the pattern is obscured by noise; too few wide classes and important detail is lost.

Explanatory and Response Variables

When an investigation explores whether one thing influences another, statisticians distinguish between two types of variable. The explanatory variable (also called the independent variable) is the one the researcher believes causes or predicts changes. The response variable (also called the dependent variable) is the outcome being measured.

Example: if you investigate whether daily revision time influences exam score, then revision time is the explanatory variable and exam score is the response variable. Plotting on a scatter graph, convention places the explanatory variable on the horizontal axis and the response variable on the vertical axis.

Key Fact

The explanatory variable goes on the horizontal (x) axis. The response variable goes on the vertical (y) axis. A memory cue: you explain how x causes changes in y.

Bivariate Data

Bivariate data is data where two measurements are taken on each individual. When you record both a student’s revision hours and their exam score, you have bivariate data — one pair of values per student. Bivariate data is used to investigate relationships: is there a correlation? Does the explanatory variable predict the response variable?

Multivariate Data (Higher)

Multivariate data is data where three or more variables are recorded for each individual. A researcher studying student performance might record revision hours, sleep duration, and exam score for each student — that is multivariate. Multivariate datasets are more realistic than bivariate ones, because real-world outcomes rarely have just a single influence.

The challenge with multivariate data is distinguishing the effect of one variable from the effects of others. If students who revise more also sleep more, it becomes difficult to say whether the exam improvement is due to revision, sleep, or both. This is why large data sets and statistical controls matter in real research.

Sometimes a questionnaire produces too many small categories. If ten students rate their commute as “less than 5 minutes”, thirty as “5–10 minutes”, and two as “50–60 minutes”, the very small categories make charts hard to read and comparisons unreliable.

Merging categories — such as combining “less than 5 minutes” and “5–10 minutes” into “up to 10 minutes” — can make the data more useful. The trade-off is that you lose detail. A good class interval choice balances readability with preserving the shape of the distribution.
exam_tip_html: On ‘State/Name’ questions that ask you to classify data, be precise: do not write “numerical” when the answer is “discrete” or “continuous”. The examiner is testing whether you know the specific term. For ‘Explain’ questions, a common error is saying “discrete data has whole numbers” — this is nearly always true but not the definition. The definition is that discrete data can only take specific separate values. Shoe sizes are discrete but include halves. On questions about explanatory and response variables, always state which axis each goes on — this earns the method mark even if you misidentify which variable is which.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Quantitative data takes numerical values; qualitative data describes categories or qualities — the key test is whether meaningful arithmetic can be performed.
  • Discrete data takes only specific separate values (e.g. number of goals); continuous data can take any value within a range (e.g. height in cm). This distinction determines which graphical representations are appropriate.
  • The explanatory (independent) variable goes on the horizontal axis; the response (dependent) variable goes on the vertical axis — bivariate data records both for each individual to investigate relationships.

practice_questions.text:
A researcher records the following for each participant in a study: their age in years, whether they own a pet (yes/no), and the number of times they visited a GP in the past year.
Which of these variables is qualitative?
A) Age in years
B) Whether they own a pet
C) Number of GP visits
D) All three are quantitative
practice_questions.marks: B [1 mark] — Pet ownership (yes/no) is qualitative categorical data. Age and GP visits are quantitative.

practice_questions.text:
State whether each of the following is discrete or continuous data.
(a) The number of text messages sent by a student in one day.
(b) The time, in minutes, taken to complete a maths test.
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Discrete [1 mark] — the number of texts can only be a whole number; there are no intermediate values.
(b) Continuous [1 mark] — time can take any value within a range, including fractions of a minute.

practice_questions.text:
A student investigates whether the distance a student lives from school affects the number of days they are absent per year. She plots a scatter graph and draws a line of best fit.
Write down which variable is the explanatory variable and which is the response variable. Explain which axis each should be plotted on.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each correct identification and 1 mark for each correct axis assignment, up to 4 marks.
Explanatory variable: distance from school [1 mark] — plotted on the horizontal (x) axis [1 mark].
Response variable: number of days absent [1 mark] — plotted on the vertical (y) axis [1 mark].
Accept 'independent variable' for explanatory and 'dependent variable' for response.

practice_questions.text:
A survey asks students to rate their enjoyment of school on a scale: poor / fair / good / excellent.
State the type of data this produces and explain one limitation of this data type for statistical analysis.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 2 marks per developed point, up to 4 marks.
Mastering: Correct data type with a precisely explained limitation.
- Type: ordinal data [1 mark] — the responses have a clear order but the gaps between categories are not necessarily equal [1 mark].
- Limitation: because the intervals are unequal, calculating the mean is not meaningful — the mean of 'poor' and 'excellent' depends on how you code them numerically, which is arbitrary [2 marks].
Secure: Correct type; limitation stated but not developed.
Developing: Names a broad category (qualitative/categorical) without identifying ordinal.
Emerging: Describes the scale without classifying it.

practice_questions.text:
A health researcher collects the following data for each participant: their age, their gender, their daily step count, their average nightly sleep in hours, and their self-rated health score (1–10).
Suggest and justify why this dataset should be described as multivariate rather than bivariate.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for identifying that more than two variables are recorded per person, and up to 4 further marks for a justified explanation.
Mastering: Clear statement that multivariate data records three or more variables per individual [1], with justification that explains the analytical advantage or distinction from bivariate [up to 4].
- Five variables are recorded for each participant (age, gender, step count, sleep, health score) [1].
- Bivariate data only records two variables per individual, allowing analysis of one pairwise relationship (e.g. sleep and health score) [1].
- Multivariate data allows investigation of how multiple explanatory variables interact — for example, whether both step count and sleep independently predict health score, or whether the effect of one disappears when the other is controlled for [1+1].
- This reflects more realistic conditions where outcomes have multiple influences [1].
Secure: Correct identification with partial justification.
Developing: States the number of variables without explaining what multivariate means.
Emerging: Confuses bivariate and multivariate.

practice_questions.text: Discuss whether it is always possible to give a clear classification of data as either quantitative or qualitative. Use examples to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for a balanced discussion with examples and a judgement.
Mastering: Two or more examples where classification is clear, at least one example where classification is ambiguous, and a concluding judgement.
- Clear quantitative: weight in kg, temperature in Celsius — arithmetic operations are clearly meaningful [1+1].
- Clear qualitative: eye colour, nationality — no meaningful average can be computed [1+1].
- Ambiguous: Likert scale responses (1 = strongly disagree, 5 = strongly agree) — these are coded numbers but the gaps between them are not equal, so treating them as quantitative is controversial; statisticians disagree on this [1+1].
- Judgement: classification is usually straightforward, but coded qualitative data creates genuine ambiguity that requires a decision about what analysis is appropriate [1].
Secure: Two contrasting examples with partial development.
Developing: One example with limited analysis.
Emerging: Defines quantitative and qualitative without using examples.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of data can only take specific, separate values with no intermediate values possible?
In an investigation into whether revision hours affect exam scores, which variable is the response variable?
Data that describes qualities or categories and cannot be meaningfully expressed as a number is called _____ data.
The _____ variable is plotted on the horizontal axis of a scatter graph and is thought to influence the other variable.
Match each data type to the correct example:
right: Number of students in a class
Survey responses: poor / fair / good / excellent

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key test for whether data is quantitative?
flashcard_questions.a: Meaningful arithmetic (such as calculating a mean) can be performed on the values.

flashcard_questions.q: What distinguishes discrete data from continuous data?
flashcard_questions.a: Discrete data can only take specific separate values; continuous can take any value in a range.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of discrete quantitative data.
flashcard_questions.a: Number of goals scored in a match.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of continuous quantitative data.

flashcard_questions.a: Data that can be ordered or ranked, but where gaps between positions are not equal.
Qualitative data that falls into named groups with no natural ordering between them.

flashcard_questions.q: In a scatter graph, which variable goes on the horizontal axis?

flashcard_questions.a: Data where two variables are recorded for each individual, used to investigate relationships.

flashcard_questions.q: The explanatory variable is also known as the _____ variable.
Why does grouping continuous data into class intervals lose precision?
flashcard_questions.a: Individual values are hidden within intervals, so the mean can only be estimated, not calculated exactly.
Data where three or more variables are recorded for each individual.

glossary_terms.definition: Data that can be measured or counted and expressed as a number.
Data that describes qualities or categories and cannot be meaningfully expressed as a number.
Data that falls into distinct named groups with no natural order between them.
Data where values can be placed in a meaningful order or rank, but the gaps between positions are not necessarily equal.
Quantitative data that can only take specific, separate values with no intermediate values possible.
Quantitative data that can take any value within a range, including fractions and decimals, limited only by the precision of measurement.
The variable that is thought to influence or explain changes in another variable; also called the independent variable.
The variable that is measured or observed and is expected to change in response to the explanatory variable; also called the dependent variable.
Data where two variables are recorded for each individual, allowing the investigation of a possible relationship between them.
Data where three or more variables are recorded for each individual, allowing the investigation of more complex relationships among multiple variables.
